# Copper December 2011 

- As this is our last copper report of 2011, we would like to take this opportunity of extending our best wishes to our readers along with our hopes for a prosperous 2012.  This past year will be remembered as a particularly volatile one, not just for copper, but for most of the commodities markets.  In the case of the red metal, having peaked at $10,148/t in February, a rocky couple of autumn months led to the erosion of one third of this value such that by early October, prices had fallen to $6785/t.  Since then, cash quotes have oscillated between $7000/t and $8000/t with most rallies short-lived by wave after wave of unsettling macro news, mostly related to the European debt crisis. 

- Despite the bearish tone to economic sentiment which has led us to defer some demand growth from 2012, we still expect the market to remain in deficit next year, partly as a result of changes on the supply side caused by slower start ups and commissioning delays at a number of projects.  Assuming that this proves to be correct, this will mark a third year of global deficit and will result in metal stocks moving lower, to 46 days on account of the 207kt shortfall in refined production relative to demand in our latest forecast.  Cash prices are expected to average $8488/t in 2012. 

- The end to the year has given us the opportunity to reflect on a year which started with demand booming in western Europe but _apparently_ very weak in China, which ironically is almost exactly the opposite now.  While Chinese demand isn’t quite booming right now, we revealed that a major de-stock was taking place earlier in the year which massively underestimated real demand.  Europe started the year with a good deal of confidence as rod mills pumped out healthy quantities of wire rod but are now looking to the new year for new impetus.  We now estimate that global demand rose by 3.5% in 2011 and forecast growth of 3.7% in 2012. 

- Confusion reigns supreme in the long-term copper concentrate market Mating Season with three sets of terms now competing for the annual benchmark.  Key contributors to this confusion are Chinese smelters who have lacked a consistent approach in their negotiating strategies thus far.  Meanwhile, Japanese smelters are seemingly adopting a tough stance, as they feel that they have already established their benchmark with Freeport.

Copper Monthly Update 

## Market Developments 

**A volatile year for the copper market draws to a close** As this is our last copper report of 2011, we would like to take this opportunity of extending our best wishes to our readers along with our hopes for a prosperous 2012.  This past year will be remembered as a particularly volatile one, not just for copper, but for most of the commodities markets.  In the case of the red metal, having peaked at $10148/t in February, a rocky couple of autumn months led to the erosion of one third of this value such that by early October, prices had fallen to $6785/t.  Since then, cash quotes have oscillated between $7000/t and $8000/t with most rallies short-lived by wave after wave of unsettling macro news, mostly related to the European debt crisis. 

As we wrote the November monthly report, there was a sharp run up in prices towards the end of October on hopes for a resolution to debt problems.  As Europe’s debt problems have moved beyond a saga or tome to a now voluminous catalogue it came as no surprise to us that the broad reason for a sharp rally in prices was related to a further debt deal, although this time with the new twist that central bankers around the world had now teamed up to ease banks’ funding requirements.  This led to a sharp 5% surge in copper prices, with cash quotes gaining just under $400/t on the final day of November to climb to $7859.5/t.  The rest of the month mirrored developments in November, with prices broadly trending lower despite the odd upward blip on positive economic releases.  Those which drew particular attention were lower unemployment figures in the US on the 16<sup>th</sup> December, although in line with prices ebbing lower through the month, less positive economic data was in the ascendancy, with China’s PMI slipping below the 50 expansion threshold as one example.  China had clearly seen this coming and had cut banks’ reserve requirements by 50 basis points the prior day in a move which underscored the fact that authorities there will likely act decisively to prevent a hard landing for the economy.  This, more than anything, should support global demand and also prices of the red metal as we head into 2012, a year we expect to be the third consecutive with the copper balance in deficit. 

**A short look at open interest** Interestingly, the final week of November was the first time that longs had added net positions since the final week of October, with the both the intermittent and following weeks characterised either by longs liquidating their positions or new shorts entering the market.  Since the end of November movements in open interest and prices suggest that new shorts are in the majority. 

**Freeport sees end to strike in Indonesia** The strike in Indonesia, wh

ich was recently resolved (December 14th ) will have been a costly one for its owners; we estimate that the overall loss of production amounts to ~100kt of copper and over 200koz of gold. While this has been by far the most significant loss in 2011, other mines, such as Cerro Verde, Escondida and El Teniente, were also disrupted to varying degrees on account of labour unrest during the year. In this context there is a large number of labour contracts due for renewal in 2012, including Hudbay’s Canadian operations and Quebrada Blanca in January; the Horne smelter in March; El Tesoro and Lomas Bayas in April; Gibraltar in May; Antamina and El Abra in July; Andina, Cuajone, Toquepala and the Ilo smelter in November; Mount Polley, Los Bronces, El Soldado and the Chagres smelter in December. The combined mine output from the aforementioned operations amounts to in excess of 1.9Mt of copper, which is a substantial tonnage that potentially will be exposed to losses on account of labour disputes. #### **Copper exchange stocks and cash LME price** 1800 10000

**China’s November imports hit year high** While it is fair to say that economic news tended to drive the market last month, with this being mostly negative, there was at least some positive market related news over the past month, with this in the shape of Chinese cathode imports. Shipments into China have been on the rise since they hit their nadir for the year in May. November’s number was particularly notable, rising by almost 48%, year on year to 343.9kt, which is the highest level since June 2009. This late surge in cathode imports has seen the cumulative figure increase to 2.4Mt which is down by 9.9% on the same 11-month period last year. However, on a net import basis the shortfall between 2011 and 2010 widens to almost 15% due to a far higher level of exports this year. We have discussed on these pages previously the rationale behind th

e continued increases in imports into China but to summarise, we believe that a combination of factors are combining to drive imports higher; most notably these are slowing domestic refined production, tighter availability of scrap and using copper for financing purposes. #### **Copper spot premia ($/t)** 200 W Europe Shanghai US c/lb 10

**Premia move lower across key markets with the exception of the US** As we described the outcome of annual premia settlements last month, we noted that the discount for each of the major regions related to expectations for demand within each of those areas. Europe achieved the greatest discount on expectations of the worst outlook for short-term consumption. This is also reflected in current premia, with rates in Europe now as low as $25-35/t, compared to $35-55/t at the end of last month, which is indeed a true reflection of extremely lackluster trade. In China, premia have edged slightly lower, but still at relatively elevated levels, to $100-130/t from $110-140/t at the end of November. Meanwhile in the US, premia have edged up slightly at 5.0-5.5 c/lb, from 4.5-5.0c/lb. Metals Market Service Monthly Update - December 2011 Page 3 of 21 Copper Monthly Update **Stock sliding away** Stocks have been sliding lower across the key exchanges but none in a more consistent manner than on the LME, which have been in almost continuous decline since October and hitting 370,850 tonnes on December 17th , their lowest level so far this year. In the intervening period, stocks had defied expectations by continuing to rise, despite broad market agreement at the start of the year of a deficit which suggested the opposite. Stock levels peaked at 477,925 tonnes on June 9th and remained stubbornly high until October when they began their descent. This was largely led by a decline in stocks at Asian locations which began tentatively in June in line with increasing Chinese imports. Material held at Asian locations has declined by c.120kt from the end of June to the end of November, with increases in European stocks initially offsetting this and stymieing downward movement in overall stock levels. In Europe, inventories remain relatively elevated and have only crept lower by c.7kt to c.51kt since the end of October, while those in US warehouses are relatively stable. Elsewhere, SHFE stocks have bounced a little higher to 79,570 tonnes from 65,205 tonnes at the end of the last month, while COMEX inventories have remained stable at c.79kt. **Market remains in deficit in 2012** Cash copper prices in 2011 are set to average around $4.00/lb, or perhaps a hair less than this, depe

nding on how the last few days of this month play out. Despite the bearish tone to economic sentiment which has led us to defer some demand growth from 2012, we still expect the market to remain in deficit next year, partly as a result of changes on the supply side caused by slower start ups and commissioning delays at a number of projects. Assuming that this proves to be correct, this will mark a third year of global deficit and will result in metal stocks moving lower, to 46 days on account of the 207kt shortfall in refined production relative to demand in our latest forecast. We do not, therefore, expect the market to move into surplus until 2013, when an upturn in global consumption growth will be outpaced by an even stronger gain in refined production. Following three years of deficits, despite a modest projected surplus, the market will remain fundamentally tight in 2013, basis 49 metal stock days and as a result, prices should remain well supported. At first sight our 2013 price projection of $8600/t ($3.90/lb), which is higher than our 2012 forecast of $8488/t ($3.85/lb), may seem a little inconsistent with our market balances and overall stock levels. However, it should be borne in mind that current negative sentiment is weighing heavily on most commodity markets and we expect a continuation of this through at least the first quarter, which will drag down next year’s average price. **Weight for it** With the full year forecast outlined above, it is also worth bearing in mind the shorter term influences on Q1 2012, including index reweighting and the Chinese Spring Festival. For copper, the reweighting of commodity indices is likely to be a relatively subdued affair with a small reduction in the weight of copper in the Dow Jones UBS index and a very slight increase in S&P GSCI index and as such, little in the way of price volatility from futures trading thus far or into January is expected from this event. Meanwhile, the 2012 Chinese Spring Festival comes earlier than usual on 23rd January, compared to early February this year. This may delay the historical pattern of the annual opening of the arbitrage window until February, when Chinese buyers return to the market in earnest, thus potentially capping LME prices in January. The other effect will be on Chinese statistical data which in comparison to this year should appear relatively poor in January and considerably better in February. **Price forecasts and world quarterly supply/demand balance – (kt)** |||**Refined**

While Chinese demand isn’t quite booming right now, we revealed that a major destock was taking place earlier in the year which massively underestimated real demand. Europe started the year with a good deal of confidence as rod mills pumped out healthy quantities of wire rod but are now looking to the new year for new impetus, while the US seems to be bumping along between those two extremes. We now estimate that global demand rose by 3.5% in 2011 and forecast growth of 3.7% in 2012. ### **Europe and CIS** **Economic activity hits the brakes** The good news revealed in eurozone industrial production data over the past month was that at least activity isn’t contracting any further following the 2% month-on-month fall in September’s reading. Moreover, it could even be said that the 1.6% year-on-year gain in October’s output was still relatively upbeat given that sentiment is crashing, however, IP growth has averaged c.5% this year, and as such, the latest figure does indeed represent a sharp slowdown in industrial activity. **Sharp slowdown in semis orders** Semis order levels have continued their trend from the past few months, with a good deal of reticence to purchase goods and place orders amid uncertainty surrounding the future of the eurozone. This is of course is further accentuated by companies nearing their financial year ends to result in stock levels through the supply chain hitting rock bottom. This could well lead to a modest boost to demand from restocking at some point if consumer and business confidence were to return, although for this to happen a more concrete resolution to the debt crisis is required. Experience tells us that is unlikely though as even when a resolution appears to have been settled, something new comes along to quash any optimism. **Italian semis shipments slide lower** Somewhat worryingly, the slowdown in IP that we discussed above happened largely after the third quarter of the year, but Q3 Italian semis shipments were already contra

cting by that stage as its economy shrank by 0.2% during the Q3 period (the first time this has occurred since 2009). Total copper and copper alloy semis production fell by 5.8% year on year in the third quarter to 229.9kt, with copper semis output dragging the overall figure lower. Copper alloy semis production came in with a reasonable 0.6% year-on-year growth rate but copper semis fell sharply, down by 10.6% year-on-year. Although the trend has been in place for much of the past two years, the better performance of copper alloys relative to pure copper semis is perhaps indicative of ongoing substitution owing to the still relatively high price of the red metal. #### **Italian semis production – (kt)** 40 360

**European premia down on sluggish demand** We noted above that semis production and orders has turned sharply lower as we near the year end, and this is unsurprisingly feeding through into cathode trade and demand. As a result, European premia have moved sharply lower, with material now changing hands for between $25-35/t, compared to $3555/t at the end of November. Metals Market Service Monthly Update - December 2011 Page 5 of 21 Copper Monthly Update **European patient in (con)traction in 2012** Overall European growth in refined demand is estimated to have grown by 3.4% in 2011, which sounds reasonable enough were it not for the fact that much of this was simply down to tax changes in Russia boosting domestic production of semis at the expense of cathode exports. This resulted in a sharp rise in domestic refined copper consumption, with Russian demand estimated to have grown by 64% in 2011. As Russian growth will return to a more “normal” pattern next year there will be nothing to artificially lift European consumption. Given the negative economic backdrop, we forecast that European copper consumption will endure a modest 0.4% contraction, before recovering modestly in 2013, with an expected 2% expansion. Risks to this forecast are heavily weighted towards to downside, however. ### **Americas** **US housing and labour markets show surprising resilience in November** The US Dept of Commerce issued pretty upbeat preliminary estimates of select construction data on December 20th , and these were followed by equally positive unemployment data released on the same day. Both inputs combined to take price-setters off guard and send stock markets and base/precious metals prices soaring on the day, which was in stark contrast to the widespread bearish views held for most of the month. First came the news from the US Dept of Commerce that building permits issued to privately-owned dwellings,

at 681k across the country, were 5.7% up on the revised figure for October (644k) and 20.7% up on the same month of a year ago (564k). Single-unit structures, which accounted for 64% of all permits issued, were up by 1.6% on October, and up by 3.6% from November 2010, while five-unit structures were up by 80.6% (to 224k) on a year ago. Equally, new housing starts at 685k in November jumped by 9.3% on October’s 627k and by 24.3% on November 2010. Starts on single-unit structures rose by 2.3% over the prior month, but fell by 1.5% on November 2010, with the main contributor to that 24.3% leap in overall starts being the surge in 5-unit structure starts (230k from just 82k a year ago). Concurrently, almost, the US Dept of Labor issued a statement saying that the national jobless rate fell by 0.4% in November, to stand at 8.6%. This compares with 9.8% of a year ago, with 45 states registering reductions from that year-ago period and 43 states showing lower unemployment rate since October. **Rod output holds steady into October, shipments improve** The above datasets could prove interesting for copper rod and wire production as we enter the final two months of the year. Typically, we would experience a seasonal slowdown during Q4, but the most recent industry sectoral data available from the American Bureau of Metal Statistics (ABMS) at least shows copper rod production just about holding on to recent levels at 105.1kt vs. 106.5kt for September and 105.4kt for October 2010. Rod shipments, on the other hand, increased by over 2% month-on-month for the first time since February this year, and this brought rod inventory down to sub-22.5kt as material moves out of storage areas swiftly ahead of year-end accounting. There is little doubt that it will take an improvement in the general construction sector if copper rod production itself is to shift out of this tight recent range. And although we do not expect to see this happening this side of the New Year, data the like of which emerged this month will be the source of such optimism as we head through 2012. #### **US production and shipments of wire rod – (kt)** 150

Metals Market Service Monthly Update - December 2011 Page 6 of 21 Copper Monthly Update ### **China** **Year end slowdown fails to dent full year growth** The recent near term weakness in the Chinese market has done little to alter our view of the outlook for domestic demand. We noted in our previous monthly publication that activity in the fourth quarter has weakened at the end use and semis production level, although refined demand is being supported by tightness in the scrap market. There has also been some restocking of cathode to take advantage of relativel

y attractive prices, in addition to increased stock levels resulting from the use of copper for financing purposes. Our short term view is that weakness will certainly spread into the early part of 2012. China has of course already acted to loosen credit conditions, and we expect further moves to follow which will lead to an upturn in output from the second quarter onwards. The very strong growth seen in Q2 of this year might well make growth look less flattering in 2012, however, with better prospects for year-on-year comparisons in the second half of the year to result in full year consumption up at similar levels to 2011 of c.8%. **Wire rod production eases back** The strong upturn in wire rod output that we have noted over the past couple of months started to slow in December as projects were rushed to be completed by the end of the year. In addition, the winter season in northern China dented the progress of some projects, with the net result that cable plants reported that their orders slipped from November levels, with further sluggish bookings expected in January. However, with a more sedate pace of growth expected in the building industry, the power sector is likely to be favoured for government spending to stimulate the domestic economy. As such, we expect solid growth from the electrical and electronics sectors overall next year. **Sheet and strip production remains soft** Sheet and strip makers report that their production fell sharply on a monthon-month basis in December, with electronic component makers preferring to eat into their own inventories at the year end. This situation will likely last until the first quarter, although this shortage of stocks will then help to trigger a rebound in the Spring. **Consumer goods sector keeping it cool** Air conditioner production continues to languish in the traditionally sluggish part of the year. Major AC manufactures cut November production by 30 to 40% from last year while some mid-tier makers cut their production by 40 to 50%, with this trend set to continue into early 2012. In this context, ACR tube makers ran at low production rates in December. Indeed, some major tube makers reported that they had cut production by 25 to 30% from the high season. **Autos to enjoy sharp recovery in 2012** Although 2011 has been a year of consolidation for the transportation market in China, the outlook remains bright both in the medium and long term. This year’s growth in automobile production of c.4% is low compared to the breakneck pace of the past two years, which have seen output double, however, 2012 looks set for a double-digit rebound. This will feed directly through to better demand for copper next year from this sector. #### **Chinese production of copper semis – (kt)** 80 1100

For 2012, we expect the recovery in industrial output to continue, despite the negative global backdrop, although part of the growth will simply be base effects given the collapse in March of 2011. **Sem

is shipments set for full year decline** Shipments of wire and cable were flat in November, with little movement on either a year-on-year or month-on-month comparison.  Shipments came in at 60.4kt in November, which was 0.4% lower than the same month last year, with the extremely weak performance of the electrical sector weighing heavily, despite continued recovery in automotive.  For the year as a whole, wire and cable shipments look set to contract somewhere in the region of 0.5%, a much better turn out than can be expected for brass mill shipments which look set to decline by 4- 5% in 2011. 

**Construction set to edge higher in 2012** There was a short term boost to copper demand in the immediate aftermath of the March disaster as a result of the construction of temporary homes, however, this now seems to have run its course and construction sector demand is now slowing sharply.  The spend on the rebuild and reconstruction of affected areas is likely to be a protracted affair lasting around 5 years and as we have noted previously, will not result in a boon for sectoral demand.  We do, however, believe that there will be at least some positive impact in 2012 and in the years that follow. 

**Nuclear fall out to dent electrical sector** The electrical and electronics sector in Japan accounts for around 39% of total semis shipments but this sector is currently enduring declining demand as investment from power companies is now focussed on dealing with the implications of policy changes with respect to nuclear generation.  This is likely to be a relatively short term phenomenon though and may well result in an increase in sectoral demand from 2013 or 2014 as investment that was deferred has to take place.  The sector should also benefit from further development in the renewables sector as Japan is a major producer of solar cells.

**Transport drives recovery in 2012** The transportation sector is set to bounce back in 2012 after production this year was hit by the earthquake and resulting disruption to supply chains.  We expect production of cars to grow by 15%, with this feeding through into healthy gains in demand for copper next year; however, the longer term outlook for automotive production in Japan is far from positive.  For a number of years Japanese producers have shifted production to the markets that vehicles are sold in to, while the strength of the yen against a number of key currencies will do nothing to reverse this trend. 

**2% decline in full year demand reiterated** Developments through the year have done little to alter our expectations of full year demand and we therefore reiterate our forecast of a c.2% decline in refined copper consumption.  Our forecast for refined copper demand in Japan mirrors that of economic and industrial activity, with a recovery forecast for 2012 of c.3%, followed by a few years of similar growth rates.

This is the country’s second largest monthly total ever and follows in the wake of the all time high of 683.5kdmt achieved in September 2010. To put this into perspective, China now imports more in one month than custom smelters in Finland, the Philippines or Sweden do in an entire year. This late surge in imports means that China’s cumulative total thus far in 2011 (5.81Mdmt) is now only 2.8% behind the comparable period last year. **Mating Season very different this year in comparison with usual trend** Thus far the 2012 copper concentrate Mating Season has been unusual on a number of fronts, not least because of the significant number of contracts that already have been concluded (historically, the first settlements have typically only occurred during the closing weeks of each year). In addition, four of the major concentrate sellers have established three different sets of terms with a variety of buyers and it remains unclear which, if any of these will event

ually become the benchmark for this current Mating Season.  It appears that Freeport has concluded all of its contracts with smelters in Chile, China, India, Japan, Korea, the Philippines with TC/RCs universally agreed upon at $63.5/t & 6.35c/lb.  It also seems that the company has finalised deals with traders at terms that are referenced to these numbers.  Including tonnages that we assume will be assigned to Gresik and to Atlantic Copper, we estimate that Freeport will have priced approximately 3.5Mt of concentrates at $63.5/t & 6.35c/lb.  According to recent press reports, Germany’s Aurubis has also concluded three long-term deals with miners at this level. 

**Anglo Chile makes its mark in the negotiations** While all eyes had been on Freeport, the market’s attention was then directed towards events that were unfolding in China where another concentrate seller was said to be concluding deals, but at a different level to the Freeport numbers.   Anglo American Chile is well known for being a market leader in the blister market, but historically, its relatively small concentrate book had precluded it from becoming a price setter in this market.  However, the company is more than doubling output at its Los Bronces mine, starting in Q4 2011 and, with many of Collahuasi’s original/existing contracts now unwinding, Anglo is also absorbing its 44% share of uncommitted Collahuasi concentrates.  Taking account of the tonnage from Los Bronces not destined for the Chagres smelter, plus Mantos Blancos and Anglo’s share of Collahuasi concentrates, we estimate that the Chilean company has approximately 1.6-1.7Mt of material for sale in 2012.  This is a sizeable tonnage and Anglo has been quick to establish itself as an independent player in the market by concluding 2012 Mating Season deals with China’s CSPT smelters and one Indian buyer at $60.5/t & 6.05c/lb. 

**BHP Billiton and Codelco add a third set of numbers to the Mating Season** Elsewhere in the long-term market, BHP Billiton acting on behalf of Escondida, is thought to have struck deals in China and India at $60/t & 6c/lb, but with a 10% tonnage reduction during H2 2012.  The rationale appears to be that this undelivered tonnage will have an intrinsic value in the spot market which at the present time is considerably lower than terms being achieved in the long-term market.  If BHP Billiton were to value this unsold portion at say $30/t & 3c/lb, this would lower the effective TC/RCs on the overall tonnage to $57/t & 5.7c/lb.  Interestingly, we also hear market rumours of at least one settlement in the Codelco camp at the same level of terms as Escondida’s, but with no tonnage reduction. 

**Will we see a two-tier long-term market?** Clearly, having three sets of terms concluded in the long-term market with few followers thus far makes it difficult to establish a representative benchmark.  Indeed, matters may become even more complicated if Antofagasta is successful in obtaining TC/RC differentials b

etween its Los Pelambres and Esperanza mines.  The company is thought to be seeking a settlement of $55/t & 5.5c/lb for the former and $58/t & 5.8c/lb for the latter with lower terms being asked for Los Pelambres to reflect its higher concentrate grade.  A key factor in all of this confusion is that Chinese smelters have been the first to settle in the current Mating Season.  While this in itself is not particularly relevant, the issue is that they have lacked a consistent approach in their negotiating strategies thus far, thereby leaving themselves open to potentially more variations in settlement terms in their subsequent negotiations with other sellers.  Meanwhile, Japanese smelters are seemingly adopting a tough stance in their negotiations, as they feel that they have already established their benchmark with Freeport at $63.5/t & 6.35c/lb.  Only time will tell how the rest of this Mating Season will pan out.  What we may see is a number of holidays being declared in Japan with effectively the establishment of a two-tier market, i.e. a Japanese benchmark along with various Mating Season TC/RC outcomes elsewhere in the world. 

## Blister/anode and scrap markets 

**China scrap imports up by 7.9% year on year** According to customs statistics, China’s copper scrap imports were 430kt in November, which is an 8% uplift on the same month last year.  This growth rate mirrors what has been achieved thus far in 2011 with scrap imports during the first 11 months increasing by 7.9% to 4.24Mt.  Internal scrap supplies have reportedly improved somewhat in December and this was reflected in a widening of the No.2 scrap discount to between 3,700 and 4,600RMB/t, compared to a range of 3,500 to 4,000RMB/t in November.  This unfortunately came too late for the country’s secondary refiners with overall Chinese cathode production down to its lowest level in five months at 448kt Cu according to NBS statistics.  Although Chinese No.2 scrap spreads have widened during December, over in the US these quotes have narrowed somewhat, from 40c/lb below March Comex last month, to 36c/lb currently. 

**Southern Copper blister tender awarded in November** Following on from last month’s Southern Copper blister tender, there have been no other spot sales to our knowledge.  The winning bid in that last tender was around the $60/t mark.

## Production news 

**Freeport sees end to strike in Indonesia** After three full months of strike action and at times violent disruption, Freeport McMoRan managed to come to an agreement with the unions at its Grasberg, Indonesian copper-gold mine on December 14th.  At the outset, in mid-September, site unions were demanding pay they considered should be more closely aligned with international conditions to bring their widely-reported hourly pay of US$2-3/hr up to the range of US$20-40/hr.  In the event, they have earned a 24% hike in the first year of this new, two-year agreement, which will be followed up with a 13% raise in year two.  FCX will also pay a one-time bonus of three months of base wages for agreeing to return to work.  In return, FCX has gained signed agreements that future negotiations will be based on living costs and the competitiveness of wages locally.  FCX notes that milling operations have been suspended since October 22nd, and although repairs to pipelines are substantially complete, the company says shipments of concentrates will be limited through the end of this year.  With there also having being shots fired on a company helicopter some days after this agreement came through, there appears to be further potential for disruption even with an agreement in place.  As the mine and mill are already up and running, though, for the present time we believe Grasberg should be able to produce 20-30k dmt of concentrate this month, and we understand that via a temporary pipeline some of this has even been transported

down to the port already.  With this lengthy labour issue now having been resolved, FCX revised its Q4 group metal sales down to 800Mlbs Cu (863kt) and 105kozs gold from 915Mlbs Cu (415kt) and 305kozs gold. 

**KGHM takes over QuadraFNX** KGHM upheld its recent promise of acquiring a mid-sized Canadian copper producer by making an all-cash offer for Vancouver-based QuadraFNX.  Under the December 6th arrangement between the two companies, shareholders of QuadraFNX will receive C$15 per common share in the company, which represented a 41.3% premium to the 20-day volume weighted average share price on the TSX up to December 5th.  The total transaction value comes to c.C$3.5B, including US$500M of outstanding gross debt.  The proposed acquisition is expected to close during Q1 2012.  The board of QuadraFNX has already recommended the acquisition to shareholders, and at the time of writing there had been no higher offer from competing parties.  This move would be the first foray outside its native Poland for the world’s 9th largest copper producer. 

**Ivanhoe loses protection from Rio’s advances** A second potential corporate ownership “change” this month will neither be as welcome nor as straightforward.  On the 13th December, an independent arbitrator upheld Rio Tinto’s claim that the “Shareholder Rights Plan” put into play by Ivanhoe Mines to protect its shareholders does not apply to Rio Tinto itself.  Market observers therefore predict that Rio will pursue opportunities to buy additional shares in Ivanhoe beyond its current 49% holding without the threat of being diluted by the Rights Plan.  Currently, there is a standstill agreement in place which prevents any such move anyway, but this expires on January 18th 2012.  Rio’s most recent position has been to state that it does not intend to make a full takeover of the company, but the market sees that Ivanhoe is now more vulnerable to a takeover from Rio with little prospect of competing bidders, given Rio’s existing holding.  The prized asset is the Oyu Tolgoi copper-gold mine in Mongolia, which is now under construction and should come into production by late 2012.
